question.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
